entries.6b63146bcb876981d6d3427c550bdd9faf71bfaf: <div sID="gen843" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="24" osisID="Gen.24" sID="Gen.24"/> <div eID="gen843" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen844" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen845" type="x-p"/> Marriages and funerals are the changes of families, and the common news among the inhabitants of the villages. In the foregoing chapter we had Abraham burying his wife, here we have him marrying his son. These stories concerning his family, with their minute circumstances, are largely related, while the histories of the kingdoms of the world then in being, with their revolutions, are buried in silence; for the Lord knows those that are his. The subjoining of Isaac's marriage to Sarah's funeral (with a particular reference to it, <reference osisRef="Gen.24.67">ver. 67</reference>) shows us that as "one generation passes away another generation comes;" and thus the entail both of the human nature, and of the covenant, is preserved. Here is, I. Abraham's care about the marrying of his son, and the charge he gave to his servant about it, <reference osisRef="Gen.24.1-Gen.24.9">ver. 1-9</reference>. II. His servant's journey into Abraham's country, to seek a wife for his young master among his own relations, <reference osisRef="Gen.24.10-Gen.24.14">ver. 10-14</reference>. III. The kind providence which brought him acquainted with Rebekah, whose father was Isaac's cousin-german, <reference osisRef="Gen.24.15-Gen.24.28">ver. 15-28</reference>. IV. The treaty of marriage with her relations, <reference osisRef="Gen.24.29-Gen.24.49">ver. 29-49</reference>. V. Their consent obtained, <reference osisRef="Gen.24.50-Gen.24.60">ver. 50-60</reference>. VI. The happy meeting and marriage between Isaac and Rebekah, <reference osisRef="Gen.24.61-Gen.24.67">ver. 61</reference>, &c.).
entries.d30fc71ebe9a697e8c7e22a2a1c343ee85ea1817: <div eID="gen845" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen844" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Abraham's Charges to His Servant. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1857.)</title> <div sID="gen846" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> And Abraham was old, <hi type="italic">and</hi> well stricken in age: and the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> had blessed Abraham in all things. <hi type="super">2</hi> And Abraham said unto his eldest servant of his house, that ruled over all that he had, Put, I pray thee, thy hand under my thigh: <hi type="super">3</hi> And I will make thee swear by the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , the God of heaven, and the God of the earth, that thou shalt not take a wife unto my son of the daughters of the Canaanites, among whom I dwell: <hi type="super">4</hi> But thou shalt go unto my country, and to my kindred, and take a wife unto my son Isaac. <hi type="super">5</hi> And the servant said unto him, Peradventure the woman will not be willing to follow me unto this land: must I needs bring thy son again unto the land from whence thou camest? <hi type="super">6</hi> And Abraham said unto him, Beware thou that thou bring not my son thither again. <hi type="super">7</hi> The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> God of heaven, which took me from my father's house, and from the land of my kindred, and which spake unto me, and that sware unto me, saying, Unto thy seed will I give this land; he shall send his angel before thee, and thou shalt take a wife unto my son from thence. <hi type="super">8</hi> And if the woman will not be willing to follow thee, then thou shalt be clear from this my oath: only bring not my son thither again. <hi type="super">9</hi> And the servant put his hand under the thigh of Abraham his master, and sware to him concerning that matter. <div eID="gen846" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen847" type="x-p"/> Three things we may observe here concerning Abraham:— <div eID="gen847" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen848" type="x-p"/> I. The care he took of a good son, to get him married, well married. It was high time to think of it now, for Isaac was about forty years old, and it had been customary with his ancestors to marry at thirty, or sooner, <reference osisRef="Gen.11.14">ch. xi. 14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.11.18">18</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.11.22">22,</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.11.24">24</reference>. Abraham believed the promise of the building up of his family, and therefore did not make haste; not more haste than good speed. Two considerations moved him to think of it now (<reference osisRef="Gen.24.1">v. 1</reference>):—1. That he himself was likely to leave the world quickly, for he was <hi type="italic">old, and well-stricken in age,</hi> and it would be a satisfaction to him to see his son settled before he died; and, 2. That he had a good estate to leave behind him, for <hi type="italic">the Lord had blessed him in all things;</hi> and the blessing of the Lord makes rich. See how much religion and piety befriend outward prosperity. Now Abraham's pious care concerning his son was, (1.) That he should not marry a daughter of Canaan, but one of his kindred. He saw that the Canaanites were degenerating into great wickedness, and knew by revelation that they were designed for ruin, and therefore he would not marry his son among them, lest they should be either a snare to his soul, or at least a blot to his name. (2.) That yet he should not leave the land of Canaan, to go himself among his kindred, not even for the purpose of choosing a wife, lest he should be tempted to settle there. This caution is given <reference osisRef="Gen.24.6">v. 6</reference>, and repeated, <reference osisRef="Gen.24.8">v. 8</reference>. "<hi type="italic">Bring not my son thither again,</hi> whatever comes of it. Let him rather want a wife than expose himself to that temptation." Note, Parents in disposing of their children, should carefully consult the welfare of their souls, and their furtherance in the way to heaven. Those who through grace have escaped the corruption that is in the world through lust, and have brought up their children accordingly, should take heed of doing any thing by which they may be again entangled therein and overcome, <reference osisRef="2Pet.2.20">2 Pet. ii. 20</reference>. Beware that you bring them not thither again, <reference osisRef="Heb.11.15">Heb. xi. 15</reference>. <div eID="gen848" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen849" type="x-p"/> II. The charge he gave to a good servant, probably Eliezer of Damascus, one of whose conduct, fidelity, and affection to him and his family, he had had long experience. He trusted him with this great affair, and not Isaac himself, because he would not have Isaac go at all into that country, but marry there by proxy; and no proxy so fit as this <hi type="italic">steward of his house.</hi> This matter is settled between the master and the servant with a great deal of care and solemnity. 1. The servant must be bound by an oath to do his utmost to get a wife for Isaac from among his relations, <reference osisRef="Gen.24.2-Gen.24.4">v. 2-4</reference>. Abraham swears him to it, both for his own satisfaction and for the engagement of his servant to all possible care and diligence in this matter. Thus God swears his servants to their work, that, having sworn, they may perform it. Honour is here done to the eternal God; for he it is that is sworn by, to whom alone these appeals ought to be made. And some think honour is done to the covenant of circumcision by the ceremony here used of <hi type="italic">putting his hand under his thigh.</hi> Note, Swearing being an ordinance not peculiar to the church, but common to mankind, is to be performed by such signs as are the appointments and common usages of our country, for binding the person sworn. 2. He must be clear of this oath if, when he had done his utmost, he could not prevail. This proviso the servant prudently inserted (<reference osisRef="Gen.24.5">v. 5</reference>), putting the case that the woman would not follow him; and Abraham allowed the exception, <reference osisRef="Gen.24.8">v. 8</reference>. Note, Oaths are to be taken with great caution, and the matter sworn to should be rightly understood and limited, because it is a <hi type="italic">snare to devour that which is holy, and, after vows, to make the enquiry</hi> which should have been made before. <div eID="gen849" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen850" type="x-p"/> III. The confidence he put in a good God, who, he doubts not, will give his servant success in this undertaking, <reference osisRef="Gen.24.7">v. 7</reference>. He remembers that God had wonderfully brought him out of the land of his nativity, by the effectual call of his grace; and therefore doubts not but he will succeed him in his care not to bring his son thither again. He remembers also the promise God had made and confirmed to him that he would give Canaan to his seed, and thence infers that God would own him in his endeavours to match his son, not among those devoted nations, but to one that was fit to be the mother of such a seed. "Fear not therefore; he shall send his angel before thee to make thy way prosperous." Note, 1. Those that carefully keep in the way of duty, and govern themselves by the principles of their religion in their designs and undertakings, have good reason to expect prosperity and success in them. God will cause that to issue in our comfort in which we sincerely aim at his glory. 2. God's promises, and our own experiences, are sufficient to encourage our dependence upon God, and our expectations from him, in all the affairs of this life. 3. God's angels are ministering spirits, sent forth, not only for the protection, but for the guidance, of the heirs of promise, <reference osisRef="Heb.1.14">Heb. i. 14</reference>. "<hi type="italic">He shall send his angel before thee,</hi> and then thou wilt speed well."
entries.33c54c5293f475ac83e23654b24bcc86afc3a114: <div eID="gen850" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Journey of Abraham's Servant. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1857.)</title> <div sID="gen851" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">10</hi> And the servant took ten camels of the camels of his master, and departed; for all the goods of his master <hi type="italic">were</hi> in his hand: and he arose, and went to Mesopotamia, unto the city of Nahor. <hi type="super">11</hi> And he made his camels to kneel down without the city by a well of water at the time of the evening, <hi type="italic">even</hi> the time that women go out to draw <hi type="italic">water.</hi> <hi type="super">12</hi> And he said, O <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> God of my master Abraham, I pray thee, send me good speed this day, and show kindness unto my master Abraham. 13 Behold, I stand <hi type="italic">here</hi> by the well of water; and the daughters of the men of the city come out to draw water: <hi type="super">14</hi> And let it come to pass, that the damsel to whom I shall say, Let down thy pitcher, I pray thee, that I may drink; and she shall say, Drink, and I will give thy camels drink also: <hi type="italic">let the same be</hi> she <hi type="italic">that</hi> thou hast appointed for thy servant Isaac; and thereby shall I know that thou hast showed kindness unto my master. <hi type="super">15</hi> And it came to pass, before he had done speaking, that, behold, Rebekah came out, who was born to Bethuel, son of Milcah, the wife of Nahor, Abraham's brother, with her pitcher upon her shoulder. <hi type="super">16</hi> And the damsel <hi type="italic">was</hi> very fair to look upon, a virgin, neither had any man known her: and she went down to the well, and filled her pitcher, and came up. <hi type="super">17</hi> And the servant ran to meet her, and said, Let me, I pray thee, drink a little water of thy pitcher. 18 And she said, Drink, my lord: and she hasted, and let down her pitcher upon her hand, and gave him drink. <hi type="super">19</hi> And when she had done giving him drink, she said, I will draw <hi type="italic">water</hi> for thy camels also, until they have done drinking. 20 And she hasted, and emptied her pitcher into the trough, and ran again unto the well to draw <hi type="italic">water,</hi> and drew for all his camels. <hi type="super">21</hi> And the man wondering at her held his peace, to wit whether the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> had made his journey prosperous or not. <hi type="super">22</hi> And it came to pass, as the camels had done drinking, that the man took a golden earring of half a shekel weight, and two bracelets for her hands of ten <hi type="italic">shekels</hi> weight of gold; <hi type="super">23</hi> And said, Whose daughter <hi type="italic">art</hi> thou? tell me, I pray thee: is there room <hi type="italic">in</hi> thy father's house for us to lodge in? <hi type="super">24</hi> And she said unto him, I <hi type="italic">am</hi> the daughter of Bethuel the son of Milcah, which she bare unto Nahor. <hi type="super">25</hi> She said moreover unto him, We have both straw and provender enough, and room to lodge in. <hi type="super">26</hi> And the man bowed down his head, and worshipped the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">27</hi> And he said, Blessed <hi type="italic">be</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> God of my master Abraham, who hath not left destitute my master of his mercy and his truth: I <hi type="italic">being</hi> in the way, the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> led me to the house of my master's brethren. <hi type="super">28</hi> And the damsel ran, and told <hi type="italic">them of</hi> her mother's house these things. <div eID="gen851" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen852" type="x-p"/> Abraham's servant now begins to make a figure in this story; and, though he is not named, yet much is here recorded to his honour, and for an example to all servants, who shall be honoured if, by faithfully serving God and their masters, they adorn the doctrine of Christ (compare <reference osisRef="Prov.27.18">Prov. xxvii. 18</reference> with <reference osisRef="Titus.2.10">Titus ii. 10</reference>); for there is no respect of persons with God, <reference osisRef="Col.3.24-Col.3.25">Col. iii. 24, 25</reference>. A good servant that makes conscience of the duty of his place, and does it in the fear of God, though he make not a figure in the world nor have praise of men, yet shall be owned and accepted of God and have praise of him. Observe here, <div eID="gen852" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen853" type="x-p"/> I. How faithful Abraham's servant approved himself to his master. Having received his charge, he with all expedition set out on his journey, with an equipage suitable to the object of his negotiation (<reference osisRef="Gen.24.10">v. 10</reference>), <hi type="italic">and he had all the goods of his master,</hi> that is, a schedule or particular account of them, <hi type="italic">in his hand,</hi> to show to those with whom he was to treat; for, from first to last, he consulted his master's honour. Isaac being a type of Christ, some make this fetching of a wife for him to signify the espousing of the church by the agency of his servants the ministers. The church is the bride, the Lamb's wife, <reference osisRef="Rev.21.9">Rev. xxi. 9</reference>. Christ is the bridegroom, and ministers are the friends of the bridegroom (<reference osisRef="John.3.29">John iii. 29</reference>), whose work it is to persuade souls to consent to him, <reference osisRef="2Cor.11.2">2 Cor. xi. 2</reference>. The spouse of Christ must not be of the Canaanites, but of his own kindred, born again from above. Ministers, like Abraham's servant, must lay out themselves with the utmost wisdom and care to serve their master's interest herein. <div eID="gen853" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen854" type="x-p"/> II. How devoutly he acknowledged God in this affair, like one of that happy household which Abraham had <hi type="italic">commanded to keep the way of the Lord,</hi> &c., <reference osisRef="Gen.18.19">ch. xviii. 19</reference>. He arrived early in the evening (after many days' journeying) at the place of his destination, and reposed himself by a well of water, to consider how he might manage his business for the best. And, <div eID="gen854" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen855" type="x-p"/> 1. He acknowledges God by a particular prayer (<reference osisRef="Gen.24.12-Gen.24.14">v. 12-14</reference>), wherein, (1.) He petitions for prosperity and good success in this affair: <hi type="italic">Send me good speed, this day.</hi> Note, We have leave to be particular in recommending our affairs to the conduct and care of the divine Providence. Those that would have good speed must pray for it. <hi type="italic">This day, in this affair;</hi> thus we must, in all our ways, acknowledge God, <reference osisRef="Prov.3.6">Prov. iii. 6</reference>. And, if we thus look up to God in every undertaking which we are in care about, we shall have the comfort of having done our duty, whatever the issue be. (2.) He pleads God's covenant with his master Abraham: <hi type="italic">O God of my master Abraham, show kindness to him.</hi> Note, As the children of good parents, so the servants of good masters, have peculiar encouragement in the prayers they offer to God for prosperity and success. (3.) He proposes a sign (<reference osisRef="Gen.24.14">v. 14</reference>), not by it to limit God, nor with a design to proceed no further if he were not gratified in it; but it is a prayer, [1.] That God would provide a good wife for his young master, and this was a good prayer. He knew that <hi type="italic">a prudent wife is from the Lord</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.19.14">Prov. xix. 14</reference>), and therefore that for this he will be enquired of. He desires that his master's wife might be humble and industrious woman, bred up to care and labour, and willing to put her hand to any work that was to be done; and that she might be of a courteous disposition, and charitable to strangers. When he came to seek a wife for his master, he did not go to the playhouse or the park, and pray that he might meet one there, but to <hi type="italic">the well of water,</hi> expecting to find one there well employed. [2.] That he would please to make his way, in this matter, plain and clear before him, by the concurrence of minute circumstances in his favour. Note, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> It is the comfort, as well as the belief, of a good man, that God's providence extends itself to the smallest occurrences and admirably serves its own purposes by them. Our times are in God's hand; not only events themselves, but the times of them. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> It is our wisdom, in all our affairs, to follow Providence, and folly to force it. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> It is very desirable, and that which we may lawfully pray for, while in the general we set God's will before us as our rule, that he will, by hints of providence, direct us in the way of our duty, and give us indications what his mind it. Thus he guides his people with his eye (<reference osisRef="Ps.32.8">Ps. xxxii. 8</reference>), and leads them in a plain path, <reference osisRef="Ps.27.11">Ps. xxvii. 11</reference>. <div eID="gen855" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen856" type="x-p"/> 2. God owns him by a particular providence. He decreed the thing, and it was established to him, <reference osisRef="Job.22.28">Job xxii. 28</reference>. According to his faith, so was it unto him. The answer to this prayer was, (1.) Speedy—<hi type="italic">before he had made an end of speaking</hi> (<reference osisRef="Gen.24.15">v. 15</reference>), as it is written (<reference osisRef="Isa.65.24">Isa. lxv. 24</reference>), <hi type="italic">While they are yet speaking, I will hear.</hi> Though we are backward to pray, God is forward to hear prayer. (2.) Satisfactory: the first that came to draw water was, and did, in every thing, according to his own heart. [1.] She was so well qualified that in all respects she answered the characters he wished for in the woman that was to be his master's wife, handsome and healthful, humble and industrious, very courteous and obliging to a stranger, and having all the marks of a good disposition. When she came to the well (<reference osisRef="Gen.24.16">v. 16</reference>), she went down and <hi type="italic">filled her pitcher, and came up</hi> to go home with it. She did not stand to gaze upon the strange man and his camels, but minded her business, and would not have been diverted from it but by an opportunity of doing good. She did not curiously nor confidently enter into discourse with him, but modestly answered him, with all the decorum that became her sex. What a degenerate age do we live in, in which appear all the instances of pride, luxury, and laziness, the reverse of Rebekah's character, whose daughters few are! Those instances of goodness which were then in honour are now in contempt. [2.] Providence so ordered it that she did that which exactly answered to his sign, and was wonderfully the counterpart of his proposal: she not only gave him drink, but, which was more than could have been expected, she offered her services to give his camels drink, which was the very sign he proposed. Note, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> God, in his providence, does sometimes wonderfully own the prayer of faith, and gratify the innocent desires of his praying people, even in little things, that he may show the extent of his care, and may encourage them at all times to seek to him and trust in him; yet we must take heed of being over-bold in prescribing to God, lest the event should weaken our faith rather than strengthen it. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> It is good to take all opportunities of showing a humble, courteous, charitable, disposition, because, some time or other, it may turn more to our honour and benefit than we think of; some hereby have entertained angels, and Rebekah hereby, quite beyond her expectation at this time, was brought into the line of Christ and the covenant. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> There may be a great deal of obliging kindness in that which costs but little: our Saviour has promised a reward for a cup of cold water, <reference osisRef="Matt.10.42">Matt. x. 42</reference>. <hi type="italic">Fourthly,</hi> The concurrence of providences and their minute circumstances, for the furtherance of our success in any business, ought to be particularly observed, with wonder and thankfulness, to the glory of God: <hi type="italic">The man wondered,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.24.21">v. 21</reference>. We have been wanting to ourselves, both in duty and in comfort, by neglecting to observe Providence. [3.] Upon enquiry he found, to his great satisfaction, that she was a near relation to his master, and that the family she was of was considerable, and able to give him entertainment, <reference osisRef="Gen.24.23-Gen.24.25">v. 23-25</reference>. Note, Providence sometimes wonderfully directs those that by faith and prayer seek direction from heaven in the choice of suitable yoke-fellows: happy marriages those are likely to be that are made in the fear of God; and these, we are sure, are made in heaven. <div eID="gen856" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen857" type="x-p"/> 3. He acknowledges God in a particular thanksgiving. He first paid his respects to Rebekah, in gratitude for her civility (<reference osisRef="Gen.24.22">v. 22</reference>), obliging her with such ornaments and attire as a maid, especially a bride, cannot forget (<reference osisRef="Jer.2.32">Jer. ii. 32</reference>), which yet, we should think, ill suited the <hi type="italic">pitcher of water;</hi> but the ear-rings and bracelets she sometimes wore did not make her think herself above the labours of a virtuous woman (<reference osisRef="Prov.31.13">Prov. xxxi. 13</reference>), who <hi type="italic">works willingly with her hands;</hi> nor the services of a child, who, while <hi type="italic">under age, differs nothing from a servant,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gal.4.1">Gal. iv. 1</reference>. Having done this, he turns his wonder (<reference osisRef="Gen.24.21">v. 21</reference>) into worshipping: <hi type="italic">Blessed be the Lord God of my master Abraham,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.24.26-Gen.24.27">v. 26, 27</reference>. Observe here, (1.) He had prayed for good speed (<reference osisRef="Gen.24.12">v. 12</reference>), and now that he had sped well he gives thanks. Note, What we win by prayer we must wear with praise; for mercies in answer to prayer lay us under particular obligations. (2.) He had as yet but a comfortable prospect of mercy, and was not certain what the issue might prove; yet he gives thanks. Note, When God's favours are coming towards us we must meet them with our praises. (3.) He blesses God for success when he was negotiating for his master. Note, We should be thankful for our friend's mercies as for our own. (4.) He gives thanks that, being in the way, at a loss what course to steer, the Lord had led him. Note, In doubtful cases, it is very comfortable to see God leading us, as he led Israel in the wilderness by the pillar of cloud and fire. (5.) He thinks himself very happy, and owns God in it, that he was led to the <hi type="italic">house of his master's brethren,</hi> those of them that had come out of Ur of the Chaldees, though they had not come to Canaan, but remained in Haran. They were not idolaters, but worshippers of the true God, and inclinable to the religion of Abraham's family. Note, God is to be acknowledged in providing suitable yoke-fellows, especially such as are agreeable in religion. (6.) He acknowledges that God, herein, had not left his master <hi type="italic">destitute of his mercy and truth.</hi> God had promised to build up Abraham's family, yet it seemed destitute of the benefit of that promise; but now Providence is working towards the accomplishing of it. Note, [1.] God's faithful ones, how destitute soever they may be of worldly comforts, shall never be left destitute of God's mercy and truth; for God's mercy is an inexhaustible fountain, and his truth an inviolable foundation. [2.] It adds much to the comfort of any blessing to see in it the continuance of God's mercy and truth.
entries.64e8ccb852b706fbff6edfdcceb63b136adfd363: <div eID="gen857" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Abraham's Servant Entertained by Laban; Errand of Abraham's Servant. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1857.)</title> <div sID="gen858" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">29</hi> And Rebekah had a brother, and his name <hi type="italic">was</hi> Laban: and Laban ran out unto the man, unto the well. 30 And it came to pass, when he saw the earring and bracelets upon his sister's hands, and when he heard the words of Rebekah his sister, saying, Thus spake the man unto me; that he came unto the man; and, behold, he stood by the camels at the well. 31 And he said, Come in, thou blessed of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; wherefore standest thou without? for I have prepared the house, and room for the camels. <hi type="super">32</hi> And the man came into the house: and he ungirded his camels, and gave straw and provender for the camels, and water to wash his feet, and the men's feet that <hi type="italic">were</hi> with him. <hi type="super">33</hi> And there was set <hi type="italic">meat</hi> before him to eat: but he said, I will not eat, until I have told mine errand. And he said, Speak on. <hi type="super">34</hi> And he said, I <hi type="italic">am</hi> Abraham's servant. <hi type="super">35</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath blessed my master greatly; and he is become great: and he hath given him flocks, and herds, and silver, and gold, and menservants, and maidservants, and camels, and asses. 36 And Sarah my master's wife bare a son to my master when she was old: and unto him hath he given all that he hath. <hi type="super">37</hi> And my master made me swear, saying, Thou shalt not take a wife to my son of the daughters of the Canaanites, in whose land I dwell: 38 But thou shalt go unto my father's house, and to my kindred, and take a wife unto my son. <hi type="super">39</hi> And I said unto my master, Peradventure the woman will not follow me. <hi type="super">40</hi> And he said unto me, The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , before whom I walk, will send his angel with thee, and prosper thy way; and thou shalt take a wife for my son of my kindred, and of my father's house: <hi type="super">41</hi> Then shalt thou be clear from <hi type="italic">this</hi> my oath, when thou comest to my kindred; and if they give not thee <hi type="italic">one,</hi> thou shalt be clear from my oath. <hi type="super">42</hi> And I came this day unto the well, and said, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> God of my master Abraham, if now thou do prosper my way which I go: <hi type="super">43</hi> Behold, I stand by the well of water; and it shall come to pass, that when the virgin cometh forth to draw <hi type="italic">water,</hi> and I say to her, Give me, I pray thee, a little water of thy pitcher to drink; <hi type="super">44</hi> And she say to me, Both drink thou, and I will also draw for thy camels: <hi type="italic">let</hi> the same <hi type="italic">be</hi> the woman whom the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath appointed out for my master's son. 45 And before I had done speaking in mine heart, behold, Rebekah came forth with her pitcher on her shoulder; and she went down unto the well, and drew <hi type="italic">water</hi>: and I said unto her, Let me drink, I pray thee. <hi type="super">46</hi> And she made haste, and let down her pitcher from her <hi type="italic">shoulder,</hi> and said, Drink, and I will give thy camels drink also: so I drank, and she made the camels drink also. <hi type="super">47</hi> And I asked her, and said, Whose daughter <hi type="italic">art</hi> thou? And she said, The daughter of Bethuel, Nahor's son, whom Milcah bare unto him: and I put the earring upon her face, and the bracelets upon her hands. 48 And I bowed down my head, and worshipped the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and blessed the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> God of my master Abraham, which had led me in the right way to take my master's brother's daughter unto his son. <hi type="super">49</hi> And now if ye will deal kindly and truly with my master, tell me: and if not, tell me; that I may turn to the right hand, or to the left. <hi type="super">50</hi> Then Laban and Bethuel answered and said, The thing proceedeth from the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : we cannot speak unto thee bad or good. 51 Behold, Rebekah <hi type="italic">is</hi> before thee, take <hi type="italic">her,</hi> and go, and let her be thy master's son's wife, as the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath spoken. <hi type="super">52</hi> And it came to pass, that, when Abraham's servant heard their words, he worshipped the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , <hi type="italic">bowing himself</hi> to the earth. <hi type="super">53</hi> And the servant brought forth jewels of silver, and jewels of gold, and raiment, and gave <hi type="italic">them</hi> to Rebekah: he gave also to her brother and to her mother precious things. <div eID="gen858" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen859" type="x-p"/> We have here the making up of the marriage between Isaac and Rebekah. It is related very largely and particularly, even to the minute circumstances, which, we should think, might have been spared, while other things of great moment and mystery (as the story of Melchizedek) are related in few words. Thus God conceals that which is curious from the wise and prudent, reveals to babes that which is common and level to their capacity (<reference osisRef="Matt.11.25">Matt. xi. 25</reference>), and rules and <hi type="italic">saves the world by the foolishness of preaching,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.21">1 Cor. i. 21</reference>. Thus also we are directed to take notice of God's providence in the little common occurrences of human life, and in them also to exercise our own prudence and other graces; for the scripture was not intended for the use of philosophers and statesmen only, but to make us all wise and virtuous in the conduct of ourselves and families. Here is, <div eID="gen859" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen860" type="x-p"/> I. The very kind reception given to Abraham's servant by Rebekah's relations. Her brother Laban went to invite and conduct him in, but not till he saw the <hi type="italic">ear-rings and the bracelets upon his sister's hands,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.24.30">v. 30</reference>. "O," thinks Laban, "here is a man that there is something to be got by, a man that is rich and generous; we will be sure to bid him welcome!" We know so much of Laban's character, by the following story, as to think that he would not have been so free of his entertainment if he had not hoped to be well paid for it, as he was, <reference osisRef="Gen.24.53">v. 53</reference>. Note, <hi type="italic">A man's gift maketh room for him</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.18.16">Prov. xviii. 16</reference>), <hi type="italic">which way soever it turneth, it prospereth,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.17.8">Prov. xvii. 8</reference>. 1. The invitation was kind: <hi type="italic">Come in, thou blessed of the Lord,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.24.31">v. 31</reference>. They saw he was rich, and therefore pronounced him <hi type="italic">blessed of the Lord;</hi> or, perhaps, because they heard from Rebekah (<reference osisRef="Gen.24.28">v. 28</reference>) of the gracious words which proceeded out of his mouth, they concluded him a good man, and therefore <hi type="italic">blessed of the Lord.</hi> Note, Those that are blessed of God should be welcome to us. It is good owning those whom God owns. 2. The entertainment was kind, <reference osisRef="Gen.24.32-Gen.24.33">v. 32, 33</reference>. Both the house and stable were well furnished, and Abraham's servant was invited to the free use of both. Particular care was taken of the camels; for a <hi type="italic">good man regardeth the life of his beast,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.12.10">Prov. xii. 10</reference>. If the ox knows his owner to serve him, the owner should know his ox to provide for him that which is fitting for him. <div eID="gen860" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen861" type="x-p"/> II. The full account which he gave them of his errand, and the court he made to them for their consent respecting Rebekah. Observe, <div eID="gen861" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen862" type="x-p"/> 1. How intent he was upon his business; though he had come off a journey, and come to a good house, he would <hi type="italic">not eat, till he had told his errand,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.24.33">v. 33</reference>. Note, The doing of our work, and the fulfilling of our trusts, either for God or man, should be preferred by us before our necessary food: it was our Saviour's meat and drink, <reference osisRef="John.4.34">John iv. 34</reference>. <div eID="gen862" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen863" type="x-p"/> 2. How ingenious he was in the management of it; he approved himself, in this matter, both a prudent man and a man of integrity, faithful to his master by whom he was trusted, and just to those with whom he now treated. <div eID="gen863" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen864" type="x-p"/> (1.) He gives a short account of the state of his master's family, <reference osisRef="Gen.24.34-Gen.24.36">v. 34-36</reference>. He was welcome before, but we may suppose him doubly welcome when he said, <hi type="italic">I am Abraham's servant.</hi> Abraham's name, no doubt, was well known among them and respected, and we might suppose them not altogether ignorant of his state, for Abraham knew theirs, <reference osisRef="Gen.22.20-Gen.22.24">ch. xxii. 20-24</reference>. Two things he suggests, to recommend his proposal:—[1.] That his master Abraham, through the blessing of God, had a very good estate; and, [2.] That he had settled it all upon Isaac, for whom he was now a suitor. <div eID="gen864" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen865" type="x-p"/> (2.) He tells them the charge his master had given him, to fetch a wife for his son from among his kindred, with the reason of it, <reference osisRef="Gen.24.37-Gen.24.38">v. 37, 38</reference>. Thus he insinuates a pleasing hint, that, though Abraham had removed to a country at so great a distance, yet he still retained the remembrance of his relations that he had left behind, and a respect for them. The highest degrees of divine affection must not divest us of natural affection. He likewise obviates an objection, That, if Isaac were deserving, he needed not send so far off for a wife: why did he not marry nearer home? "For a good reason," says he; "my master's son must not match with a Canaanite." He further recommends his proposal, [1.] From the faith his master had that it would succeed, <reference osisRef="Gen.24.40">v. 40</reference>. Abraham took encouragement from the testimony of his conscience that he <hi type="italic">walked before God</hi> in a regular course of holy living, and thence inferred that God would prosper him; probably he refers to that covenant which God had made with him (<reference osisRef="Gen.17.1">ch. xvii. 1</reference>), <hi type="italic">I am God, all-sufficient, walk before me.</hi> Therefore, says he <hi type="italic">the God before whom I walk will send his angel.</hi> Note, While we make conscience of our part of the covenant, we may take the comfort of God's part of it; and we should learn to apply general promises of particular cases, as there is occasion. [2.] From the care he himself had taken to preserve their liberty of giving or refusing their consent, as they should see cause, without incurring the guilt of perjury (<reference osisRef="Gen.24.39-Gen.24.41">v. 39-41</reference>), which showed him, in general, to be a cautious man, and particularly careful that their consent might not be forced, but be either free or not at all. <div eID="gen865" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen866" type="x-p"/> (3.) He relates to them the wonderful concurrence of providences, to countenance and further the proposal, plainly showing the finger of God in it. [1.] He tells them how he had prayed for direction by a sign, <reference osisRef="Gen.24.42-Gen.24.44">v. 42-44</reference>. Note, It is good dealing with those who by prayer take God along with them in their dealings. [2.] How God had answered his prayer in the very letter of it. Though he did but <hi type="italic">speak in his heart</hi> (<reference osisRef="Gen.24.45">v. 45</reference>), which perhaps he mentions, lest it should be suspected that Rebekah had overheard his prayer and designedly humoured it. "No," says he, "I spoke <hi type="italic">it in my heart,</hi> so that none heard it but God, to whom thought are word, and from him the answer came," <reference osisRef="Gen.24.46-Gen.24.47">v. 46, 47</reference>. [3.] How he had immediately acknowledged God's goodness to him therein, <hi type="italic">leading him,</hi> as he here expresses it, <hi type="italic">in the right way.</hi> Note, God's way is always the <hi type="italic">right way</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.107.7">Ps. cvii. 7</reference>), and those are well led whom he leads. <div eID="gen866" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen867" type="x-p"/> (4.) He fairly refers the matter to their consideration, and waits their decision (<reference osisRef="Gen.24.49">v. 49</reference>): "<hi type="italic">If you will deal kindly and truly with my master,</hi> well and good: if you will be sincerely kind, you will accept the proposal, and I have what I came for; if not, do not hold me in suspense." Note, Those who deal fairly have reason to expect fair dealing. <div eID="gen867" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen868" type="x-p"/> (5.) They freely and cheerfully close with the proposal upon a very good principle (<reference osisRef="Gen.24.50">v. 50</reference>): "<hi type="italic">The thing proceedeth from the Lord,</hi> Providence smiles upon it, and we have nothing to say against it." They do not object distance of place, Abraham's forsaking them, or his having no land in possession, but personal estate only: they do not question the truth of what this man said; but, [1.] They trust much to his integrity. It were well if honesty did so universally prevail among men that it might be as much an act of prudence as it is of good nature to take a man's word. [2.] They trust more to God's providence, and therefore by silence give consent, because it appears to be directed and disposed by Infinite Wisdom. Note, A marriage is then likely to be comfortable when it appears to proceed from the Lord. <div eID="gen868" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen869" type="x-p"/> (6.) Abraham's servant makes a thankful acknowledgment of the good success he had met with, [1.] To God: <hi type="italic">He worshipped the Lord,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.24.52">v. 52</reference>. Observe, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> As his good success went on, he went on to bless God. Those that <hi type="italic">pray without ceasing</hi> should <hi type="italic">in every thing give thanks,</hi> and own God in every step of mercy. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> God sent his angel before him, and so gave him success, <reference osisRef="Gen.24.7">v. 7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.24.40">40</reference>. But when he has the desired success, he worships God, not the angel. Whatever benefit we have by the ministration of angels, all the glory must be given to the Lord of the angels, <reference osisRef="Rev.22.9">Rev. xxii. 9</reference>. [2.] He pays his respects to the family also, and particularly to the bride, <reference osisRef="Gen.24.53">v. 53</reference>. He presented her, and her mother, and brother, with many precious things, both to give a real proof of his master's riches and generosity and in gratitude for their civility to him, and further to ingratiate himself with them.
entries.0ab0ecfdaf0cc18a06f6c539b153a2e7adf060c0: <div eID="gen869" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Rebekah's Departure. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1857.)</title> <div sID="gen870" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">54</hi> And they did eat and drink, he and the men that <hi type="italic">were</hi> with him, and tarried all night; and they rose up in the morning, and he said, Send me away unto my master. <hi type="super">55</hi> And her brother and her mother said, Let the damsel abide with us <hi type="italic">a few</hi> days, at the least ten; after that she shall go. 56 And he said unto them, Hinder me not, seeing the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath prospered my way; send me away that I may go to my master. <hi type="super">57</hi> And they said, We will call the damsel, and enquire at her mouth. <hi type="super">58</hi> And they called Rebekah, and said unto her, Wilt thou go with this man? And she said, I will go. <hi type="super">59</hi> And they sent away Rebekah their sister, and her nurse, and Abraham's servant, and his men. <hi type="super">60</hi> And they blessed Rebekah, and said unto her, Thou <hi type="italic">art</hi> our sister, be thou <hi type="italic">the mother</hi> of thousands of millions, and let thy seed possess the gate of those which hate them. <hi type="super">61</hi> And Rebekah arose, and her damsels, and they rode upon the camels, and followed the man: and the servant took Rebekah, and went his way. <div eID="gen870" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen871" type="x-p"/> Rebekah is here taking leave of her father's house; and 1. Abraham's servant presses for a dismission. Though he and his company were very welcome, and very cheerful there, yet he said, <hi type="italic">Send me away</hi> (<reference osisRef="Gen.24.54">v. 54</reference>), and again, <reference osisRef="Gen.24.56">v. 56</reference>. He knew his master would expect him home with some impatience; he had business to do at home which wanted him, and therefore, as one that preferred his work before his pleasure, he was for hastening home. Note, Lingering and loitering no way become a wise and good man; when we have despatched our business abroad we must not delay our return to our business at home, nor be longer from it than needs must; for as a bird that <hi type="italic">wanders from her nest so is he that wanders from his place,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.27.8">Prov. xxvii. 8</reference>. 2. Rebekah's relations, from natural affection and according to the usual expression of kindness in that case, solicit for her stay some time among them, <reference osisRef="Gen.24.55">v. 55</reference>. They could not think of parting with her on a sudden, especially as she was about the remove so far off and it was not likely that they would ever see one another again: <hi type="italic">Let her stay a few days, at least ten,</hi> which makes it as reasonable a request as the reading in the margin seems to make it unreasonable, <hi type="italic">a year,</hi> or <hi type="italic">at least ten months.</hi> They had consented to the marriage, and yet were loth to part with her. Note, It is an instance of the vanity of this world that there is nothing in it so agreeable but it has its alloy. <hi type="italic">Nulla est sincera voluptas—There is no unmingled pleasure.</hi> They were pleased that they had matched a daughter of their family so well, and yet, when it came to the last, it was with great reluctance that they sent her away. 3. Rebekah herself determined the matter. To her they appealed, as it was fit they should (<reference osisRef="Gen.24.57">v. 57</reference>): <hi type="italic">Call the damsel</hi> (who had retired to her apartment with a modest silence) and <hi type="italic">enquire at her mouth.</hi> Note, As children ought not to marry without their parents' consent, so parents ought not to marry them without their own. Before the matter is resolved on, "Ask at the damsel's mouth;" she is a party principally concerned, and therefore ought to be principally consulted. Rebekah consented, not only to go, but to go immediately: <hi type="italic">I will go,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.24.58">v. 58</reference>. We may hope that the notice she had taken of the servant's piety and devotion gave her such an idea of the prevalence of religion and godliness in the family she was to go to made her desirous to hasten thither, and willing to forget her own people and her father's house, where religion had not so much the ascendant. 4. Hereupon she is sent away with Abraham's servant; not, we may suppose, the very next day after, but very quickly: her friends see that she has a good heart on it, and so they dismiss her, (1.) With suitable attendants—her <hi type="italic">nurse</hi> (<reference osisRef="Gen.24.59">v. 59</reference>), her <hi type="italic">damsels,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.24.61">v. 61</reference>. It seems, then, that when she went to the well for water it was not because she had not servants at command, but because she took a pleasure in works of humble industry. Now that she was going among strangers, it was fit she should take those with her with whom she was acquainted. Here is nothing said of her portion. Her personal merits were a portion in her, she needed none with her, nor did that ever come into the treaty of marriage. (2.) With hearty good wishes: <hi type="italic">They blessed Rebekah,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.24.60">v. 60</reference>. Note, When our relations are entering into a new condition, we ought by prayer to recommend them to the blessing and grace of God. Now that she was going to be a wife, they prayed that she might be a mother both of a numerous and of a victorious progeny. Perhaps Abraham's servant had told them of the promise God had lately made to his master, which it is likely, Abraham acquainted his household with, that God <hi type="italic">would multiply his seed as the stars of heaven, and that they should possess the gate of their enemies</hi> (<reference osisRef="Gen.22.17">ch. xxii. 17</reference>), to which promise they had an eye in this blessing, <hi type="italic">Be thou the mother</hi> of that seed.
entries.80b184e6da8264aa551732815bc802699cd86940: <div eID="gen871" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Isaac's Marriage. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1857.)</title> <div sID="gen872" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">62</hi> And Isaac came from the way of the well Lahai-roi; for he dwelt in the south country. <hi type="super">63</hi> And Isaac went out to meditate in the field at the eventide: and he lifted up his eyes, and saw, and, behold, the camels <hi type="italic">were</hi> coming. 64 And Rebekah lifted up her eyes, and when she saw Isaac, she lighted off the camel. <hi type="super">65</hi> For she <hi type="italic">had</hi> said unto the servant, What man <hi type="italic">is</hi> this that walketh in the field to meet us? And the servant <hi type="italic">had</hi> said, It <hi type="italic">is</hi> my master: therefore she took a veil, and covered herself. <hi type="super">66</hi> And the servant told Isaac all things that he had done. <hi type="super">67</hi> And Isaac brought her into his mother Sarah's tent, and took Rebekah, and she became his wife; and he loved her: and Isaac was comforted after his mother's <hi type="italic">death.</hi> <div eID="gen872" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen873" type="x-p"/> Isaac and Rebekah are, at length, happily brought together. Observe, <div eID="gen873" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen874" type="x-p"/> I. Isaac was well employed when he met Rebekah: <hi type="italic">He went out to meditate,</hi> or pray, <hi type="italic">in the field, at the even-tide,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.24.62-Gen.24.63">v. 62, 63</reference>. Some think he expected the return of his servants about this time, and went out on purpose to meet them. But, it should seem, he went out on another errand, to take the advantage of a silent evening and a solitary field for meditation and prayer, those divine exercises by which we converse with God and our own hearts. Note, 1. Holy souls love retirement. It will do us good to be often left alone, walking alone and sitting alone; and, if we have the art of improving solitude, we shall find we are never less alone than when alone. 2. Meditation and prayer ought to be both our business and our delight when we are alone; while we have a God, a Christ, and a heaven, to acquaint ourselves with, and to secure our interest in, we need not want matter either for meditation or prayer, which, if they go together, will mutually befriend each other. 3. Our walks in the field are then truly pleasant when in them we apply ourselves to meditation and prayer. We there have a free and open prospect of the heavens above us and the earth around us, and the host and riches of both, by the view of which we should be led to the contemplation of the Maker and owner of all. 4. The exercises of devotion should be the refreshment and entertainment of the evening, to relieve us from the fatigue occasioned by the care and business of the day, and to prepare us for the repose and sleep of the night. 5. Merciful providences are then doubly comfortable when they find us well employed and in the way of our duty. Some think Isaac was now praying for good success in this affair that was depending, and meditating upon that which was proper to encourage his hope in God concerning it; and now, when he sets himself, as it were, upon his watch-tower, to see what God would answer him, as the prophet (<reference osisRef="Hab.2.1">Hab. ii. 1</reference>), <hi type="italic">he sees the camels coming.</hi> Sometimes God sends in the mercy prayed for immediately, <reference osisRef="Acts.12.12">Acts xii. 12</reference>. <div eID="gen874" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen875" type="x-p"/> II. Rebekah behaved herself very becomingly, when she met Isaac: understanding who he was, she <hi type="italic">alighted off her camel</hi> (<reference osisRef="Gen.24.64">v. 64</reference>), and <hi type="italic">took a veil, and covered herself</hi> (<reference osisRef="Gen.24.65">v. 65</reference>), in token of humility, modesty, and subjection. She did not reproach Isaac for not coming himself to fetch her, or, at least, to meet her a day's journey or two, did not complain of the tediousness of her journey, or the difficulty of leaving her relations, to come into a strange place; but, having seen Providence going before her in the affair, she accommodates herself with cheerfulness to her new relation. Those that by faith are espoused to Christ, and would be presented as chaste virgins to him, must, in conformity to his example, humble themselves, as Rebekah, who alighted when she saw Isaac on foot, and must put themselves into subjection to him who is their head (<reference osisRef="Eph.5.24">Eph. v. 24</reference>), as Rebekah, signifying it by the veil she put on, <reference osisRef="1Cor.11.10">1 Cor. xi. 10</reference>. <div eID="gen875" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen876" type="x-p"/> III. They were brought together (probably after some further acquaintance), to their mutual comfort, <reference osisRef="Gen.24.67">v. 67</reference>. Observe here, 1. What an affectionate son he was to his mother: it was about three years since her death, and yet he was not, till now, comforted concerning it; the wound which that affliction gave to his tender spirit bled so long, and was never healed till God brought him into this new relation. Thus crosses and comforts are balances to each other (<reference osisRef="Eccl.7.14">Eccl. vii. 14</reference>), and help to keep the scale even. 2. What an affectionate husband he was to his wife. Note, Those that have approved themselves well in one relation, it may be hoped, will do so in another: <hi type="italic">She became his wife, and he loved her;</hi> there was all the reason in the world why he should, for so <hi type="italic">ought men to love their wives even as themselves.</hi> The duty of the relation is then done, and the comfort of the relation is then enjoyed, when mutual love governs; for <hi type="italic">there the Lord commands the blessing.</hi>  <chapter eID="Gen.24"/> <div eID="gen876" type="x-p"/>

entries.a8bda83daea6113fea72368b682ed2ebc92f1f49: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv254"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 24</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Gen.24.1-Gen.24.9">Ge 24:1-9</reference>. A Marriage Commission.</title> <div sID="gen431" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv254"/><hi type="bold">1. And Abraham was old ... take a wife--</hi>His anxiety to see his son married was natural to his position as a pastoral chief interested in preserving the honor of his tribe, and still more as a patriarch who had regard to the divine promise of a numerous posterity. <div eID="gen431" type="x-p"/>
entries.e7df41d29c623df7dcd80b33ec356406b310d469: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv255"/><div sID="gen432" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv255"/><hi type="bold">2. said unto his eldest servant--</hi>Abraham being too old, and as the heir of the promise not being at liberty to make even a temporary visit to his native land, was obliged to intrust this delicate mission to Eliezer, whom, although putting entire confidence in him, he on this occasion bound by a solemn oath. A pastoral chief in the present day would follow the same course if he could not go himself. <div eID="gen432" type="x-p"/>
entries.477c69b7a38fa6e14650fe0c5a999a58f43d8fc9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv256"/><div sID="gen433" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv256"/><hi type="bold">3. thou shalt not take a wife, &c.--</hi>Among pastoral tribes the matrimonial arrangements are made by the parents, and a youth must marry, not among strangers, but in his own tribe--custom giving him a claim, which is seldom or never resisted, to the hand of his first cousin. But Abraham had a far higher motive--a fear lest, if his son married into a Canaanitish family, he might be gradually led away from the true God. <div eID="gen433" type="x-p"/>
entries.b3f4ddcfea16e3b1c1e0659cfdba70fff77a8613: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv257"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Gen.24.10-Gen.24.67">Ge 24:10-67</reference>. The Journey.</title> <div sID="gen434" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv257"/><hi type="bold">10. the servant took ten camels, &c.--</hi>So great an equipage was to give the embassy an appearance worthy of the rank and wealth of Abraham; to carry provisions; to bear the marriage presents, which as usual would be distributed over several beasts; besides one or two spare camels in case of emergency.<div eID="gen434" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen435" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">went to Mesopotamia, &c.--</hi>A stranger in those regions, who wishes to obtain information, stations himself at one of the wells in the neighborhood of a town, and he is sure to learn all the news of the place from the women who frequent them every morning and evening. Eliezer followed this course, and letting his camels rest, he waited till the evening time of water drawing. <div eID="gen435" type="x-p"/>
entries.c65f6a9e91f6dd6cb4f5071e2ee481a54929c61f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv258"/><div sID="gen436" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv258"/><hi type="bold">12. And he said, O Lord God of my master--</hi>The servant appears worthy of the master he served. He resolves to follow the leading of Providence; and while he shows good sense in the tokens he fixes upon of ascertaining the temper and character of the future bride, he never doubts but that in such a case God will direct him. <div eID="gen436" type="x-p"/>
entries.873a0a1475fd0961b11c0e6c63688662ef3a3c38: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv259"/><div sID="gen437" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv259"/><hi type="bold">15-21. before he had done speaking ... behold, Rebekah came out--</hi>As he anticipated, a young woman unveiled, as in pastoral regions, appeared with her pitcher on her shoulder. Her comely appearance, her affable manners, her obliging courtesy in going down the steps to fetch water not only to him but to pour it into the trough for his camels, afforded him the most agreeable surprise. She was the very person his imagination had pictured, and he proceeded to reward her civility. <div eID="gen437" type="x-p"/>
entries.9831cfd81a08a24b7a93824f1bacbb215ade99b4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv260"/><div sID="gen438" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv260"/><hi type="bold">22. the man took a golden earring, &c.--</hi>The ring was not for the ear, but the nose; the armlets, such as young women in Syria and Arabia still appear daily at wells decked in. They are worn from the elbow to the wrist, commonly made of silver, copper, brass, or horn. <div eID="gen438" type="x-p"/>
entries.7cd2700b7ee301c160cee6ecc067a83ae211c29e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv261"/><div sID="gen439" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv261"/><hi type="bold">23-27. And said, Whose daughter art thou?--</hi>After telling her name and family, the kind-hearted damsel hastened home to give notice of a stranger's arrival. <div eID="gen439" type="x-p"/>
entries.d4c494cb96c56b3579efd3792ad7866b4fa12eb9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv262"/><div sID="gen440" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv262"/><hi type="bold">28. and told them of her mother's house these things--</hi>the female apartments. This family was in an advanced stage of pastoral life, dwelling in a settled place and a fixed habitation. <div eID="gen440" type="x-p"/>
entries.0accffd75e3749c173e2bbc3702fa251bdce21b0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv263"/><div sID="gen441" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv263"/><hi type="bold">29-31. Rebekah had a brother ... Laban ran out--</hi>From what we know of his character, there is reason to believe that the sight of the dazzling presents increased both his haste and his invitation. <div eID="gen441" type="x-p"/>
entries.7e7086d8922a9e2c1a3df0a3e4f0a31b86c0d7a7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv264"/><div sID="gen442" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv264"/><hi type="bold">32-49. the man came into the house, &c.--</hi>What a beautiful picture of piety, fidelity, and disinterestedness in a servant! He declined all attention to his own comforts till he had told his name and his errand. <div eID="gen442" type="x-p"/>
entries.2b424ec6669abdfb8afa131e5dbdcb2be1ad4ef4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv265"/><div sID="gen443" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv265"/><hi type="bold">50. Then Laban and Bethuel answered--</hi>The brothers conduct all the marriage negotiations, their father being probably dead, and without consulting their sister. Their language seems to indicate they were worshippers of the true God. <div eID="gen443" type="x-p"/>
entries.d51d6aa04ee6a2d15073c432332ada0855db0cdb: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv266"/><div sID="gen444" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv266"/><hi type="bold">53. And the servant brought forth jewels of silver, and ... gold--</hi>These are the usual articles, with money, that form a woman's dowry among the pastoral tribes. Rebekah was betrothed and accompanied the servant to Canaan. <div eID="gen444" type="x-p"/>
entries.d9aa90ccf109015bdade273f638f595500ebb577: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv267"/><div sID="gen445" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv267"/><hi type="bold">64. she lighted off the camel--</hi>If Isaac were walking, it would have been most unmannerly for her to have continued seated; an inferior, if riding, always alights in presence of a person of rank, no exception being made for women. <div eID="gen445" type="x-p"/>
entries.df3c18d69cb9a181d3c89dc6b8ef798102df1c78: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv268"/><div sID="gen446" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv268"/><hi type="bold">65. she took a veil, and covered herself--</hi>The veil is an essential part of female dress. In country places it is often thrown aside, but on the appearance of a stranger, it is drawn over the face, as to conceal all but the eyes. In a bride it was a token of her reverence and subjection to her husband. <div eID="gen446" type="x-p"/>
entries.4b5c6bad446ab42980bbd9ff2e234ec85245276b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv269"/><div sID="gen447" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv269"/><hi type="bold">67. And Isaac brought her into his mother's ... tent--</hi>thus establishing her at once in the rights and honors of a wife before he had seen her features. Disappointments often take place, but when Isaac saw his wife, "he loved her." <chapter eID="Gen.24"/>

entries.2cf10b2011571330c0adcedc2d2846b8624b6cd0: <div eID="gen1066" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen1067" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen1068" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen1068" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen1067" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen1069" type="x-p"/> Abraham, being solicitous to get his son Isaac property married, calls his confidential servant, probably Eliezer, and makes him swear that he will not take a wife for Isaac from among the Canaanites, <reference osisRef="Gen.24.1-Gen.24.3">Gen 24:1-3</reference>, but from among his own kindred, <reference osisRef="Gen.24.4">Gen 24:4</reference>. The servant proposes certain difficulties, <reference osisRef="Gen.24.5">Gen 24:5</reference>, which Abraham removes by giving him the strongest assurances of God's direction in the business, <reference osisRef="Gen.24.6">Gen 24:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.24.7">Gen 24:7</reference>, and then specifies the conditions of the oath, <reference osisRef="Gen.24.8">Gen 24:8</reference>. The form of the oath itself, <reference osisRef="Gen.24.9">Gen 24:9</reference>. The servant makes preparations for his journey, and sets out for Mesopotamia, the residence of Abraham's kindred, <reference osisRef="Gen.24.10">Gen 24:10</reference>. Arrives at a well near to the place, <reference osisRef="Gen.24.11">Gen 24:11</reference>. His prayer to God, <reference osisRef="Gen.24.12-Gen.24.14">Gen 24:12-14</reference>. Rebekah, the daughter of Bethuel, son of Nahor, Abraham's brother, comes to the well to draw water, <reference osisRef="Gen.24.15">Gen 24:15</reference>. She is described, <reference osisRef="Gen.24.16">Gen 24:16</reference>. Conversation between her and Abraham's servant, in which every thing took place according to his prayer to God, <reference osisRef="Gen.24.17-Gen.24.21">Gen 24:17-21</reference>. He makes her presents, and learns whose daughter she is, <reference osisRef="Gen.24.22-Gen.24.24">Gen 24:22-24</reference>. She invites him to her father's house, <reference osisRef="Gen.24.25">Gen 24:25</reference>. He returns thanks to God for having thus far given him a prosperous journey, <reference osisRef="Gen.24.26">Gen 24:26</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.24.27">Gen 24:27</reference>. Rebekah runs home and informs her family, <reference osisRef="Gen.24.28">Gen 24:28</reference>; on which her brother Laban comes out, and invites the servant home, <reference osisRef="Gen.24.29-Gen.24.31">Gen 24:29-31</reference>. His reception, <reference osisRef="Gen.24.32">Gen 24:32</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.24.33">Gen 24:33</reference>. Tells his errand, <reference osisRef="Gen.24.34">Gen 24:34</reference>, and how he had proceeded in executing the trust reposed in him, <reference osisRef="Gen.24.35-Gen.24.48">Gen 24:35-48</reference>. Requests an answer, <reference osisRef="Gen.24.49">Gen 24:49</reference>. The family of Rebekah consent that she should become the wife of Isaac, <reference osisRef="Gen.24.50">Gen 24:50</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.24.51">Gen 24:51</reference>. The servant worships God, <reference osisRef="Gen.24.52">Gen 24:52</reference>, and gives presents to Milcah, Laban, and Rebekah, <reference osisRef="Gen.24.53">Gen 24:53</reference>. He requests to be dismissed, <reference osisRef="Gen.24.54-Gen.24.56">Gen 24:54-56</reference>. Rebekah, being consulted, consents to go, <reference osisRef="Gen.24.57">Gen 24:57</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.24.58">Gen 24:58</reference>. She is accompanied by her nurse, <reference osisRef="Gen.24.59">Gen 24:59</reference>; and having received the blessing of her parents and relatives, <reference osisRef="Gen.24.60">Gen 24:60</reference>, she departs with the servant of Abraham, <reference osisRef="Gen.24.61">Gen 24:61</reference>. They are met by Isaac, who was on an evening walk for the purpose of meditation, <reference osisRef="Gen.24.62-Gen.24.65">Gen 24:62-65</reference>. The servant relates to Isaac all that he had done, <reference osisRef="Gen.24.66">Gen 24:66</reference>. Isaac and Rebekah are married, <reference osisRef="Gen.24.67">Gen 24:67</reference>. <div eID="gen1069" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1070" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen1070" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1071" type="x-p"/> And Abraham was old - He was now about one hundred and forty years of age, and consequently Isaac was forty, being born when his father was one hundred years old. See <reference osisRef="Gen.21.5">Gen 21:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.25.20">Gen 25:20</reference>.
entries.63e9f5bd76fed973d9ce3d6ad010f2e21ce06f12: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen1071" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1072" type="x-p"/> Eldest servant - As this eldest servant is stated to have been the ruler over all that he had, it is very likely that Eliezer is meant. See <reference osisRef="Gen.15.2">Gen 15:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.15.3">Gen 15:3</reference>. <div eID="gen1072" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1073" type="x-p"/> Put, I pray thee, thy hand - See note on <reference osisRef="Gen.24.9">Gen 24:9</reference>.
entries.ee9a9b84df7a1e927397ba6a232cc41d8bfcba81: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen1073" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1074" type="x-p"/> I will make thee swear - See note on <reference osisRef="Gen.24.9">Gen 24:9</reference>. <div eID="gen1074" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1075" type="x-p"/> Of the Canaanites - Because these had already been devoted to slavery, etc., and it would have been utterly inconsistent as well with prudence as with the design of God to have united the child and heir of the promise with one who was under a curse, though that curse might be considered to be only of a political nature. See the curse of Canaan, <reference osisRef="Gen.9.25">Gen 9:25</reference> (note).
entries.d321025752c7a668103d2b69a2676a8030bb676f: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen1075" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1076" type="x-p"/> My country - Mesopotamia, called here Abraham's country, because it was the place where the family of Haran, his brother, had settled; and where himself had remained a considerable time with his father Terah. In this family, as well as in that of Nahor, the true religion had been in some sort preserved, though afterwards considerably corrupted; see <reference osisRef="Gen.31.19">Gen 31:19</reference>. <div eID="gen1076" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1077" type="x-p"/> And take a wife unto my son - A young man in Bengal is precisely in the same circumstances as Isaac; he has nothing to do in the choice of a wife; parents employ others to seek wives for their sons. Those who leave their homes in search of employment always marry their children in their own country, and among their acquaintance at home; never among the people with whom they reside. In Asiatic countries this custom has prevailed from the infancy of the human race. See Ward's Hindoo Customs.
entries.4f26234ced674ad3fe64552be7bf77cf556ecf4c: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen1077" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1078" type="x-p"/> Peradventure the woman will not be willing - We may see, says Calmet, by this and other passages of Scripture, <reference osisRef="Jos.9.18">Jos 9:18</reference>, what the sentiments of the ancients were relative to an oath. They believed they were bound precisely by what was spoken, and had no liberty to interpret the intentions of those to whom the oath was made.
entries.e44aef47460d5d8d2f61c47d7374878b1a81ebcb: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen1078" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1079" type="x-p"/> The Lord God, etc. - He expresses the strongest confidence in God, that the great designs for which he had brought him from his own kindred to propagate the true religion in the earth would be accomplished; and that therefore, when earthly instruments failed, heavenly ones should be employed. He shall send his angel, probably meaning the Angel of the Covenant, of whom see <reference osisRef="Gen.15.7">Gen 15:7</reference>.
entries.1612fed1108c5af4af09ec5c6467493ace66941a: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen1079" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1080" type="x-p"/> Put his hand under the thigh of Abraham - This form of swearing has greatly puzzled the commentators; but it is useless to detail opinions which I neither believe myself, nor would wish my readers to credit. I believe the true sense is given in the Targum of Jonathan ben Uzziel, and that called the Jerusalem Targum. In the former it is said, Put now thy hand בגזית מהולתי bigzirath mehulathi, in sectione circumcisionis meoe; in the latter תחות ירך קימי techoth yerech keyami, sub femore foederis mei. When we put the circumstances mentioned in this and the third verse together, we shall find that they fully express the ancient method of binding by oath in such transactions as had a religious tendency. 1. The rite or ceremony used on the occasion: the person binding himself put his hand under the thigh of the person to whom he was to be bound; i.e., he put his hand on the part that bore the mark of circumcision, the sign of God's covenant, which is tantamount to our kissing the book, or laying the hand upon the New Testament or covenant of our Lord Jesus Christ. 2. The form of the oath itself: the person swore by Jehovah, the God of heaven and the God of the earth. Three essential attributes of God are here mentioned: <div eID="gen1080" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1081" type="x-p"/> 1. His self-existence and eternity in the name Jehovah. <div eID="gen1081" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1082" type="x-p"/> 2. His dominion of glory and blessedness in the kingdom of heaven. <div eID="gen1082" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1083" type="x-p"/> 3. His providence and bounty in the earth. <div eID="gen1083" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1084" type="x-p"/> The meaning of the oath seems to be this: "As God is unchangeable in his nature and purposes, so shall I be in this engagement, under the penalty of forfeiting all expectation of temporal prosperity, the benefits of the mystical covenant, and future glory." An oath of this kind, taken at such a time, and on such an occasion, can never be deemed irreligious or profane. Thou shalt swear by his name - shalt acknowledge and bind thyself unto the true God, as the just Judge of thy motives and actions, is a command of the Most High; and such an oath as the above is at once (on such an occasion) both proper and rational. The person binding himself proposes for a pattern the unchangeable and just God; and as He is the avenger of wrong and the punisher of falsehood, and has all power in the heavens and in the earth, so he can punish perjury by privation of spiritual and temporal blessings, by the loss of life, and by inflicting the perdition due to ungodly men, among whom liars and perjured persons occupy the most distinguished rank. Our ideas of delicacy may revolt from the rite used on this occasion; but, when the nature of the covenant is considered, of which circumcision was the sign, we shall at once perceive that this rite could not be used without producing sentiments of reverence and godly fear, as the contracting party must know that the God of this covenant was a consuming fire.
entries.1509d66782c9a72bd6afce07cb9bd4f6a3e261dc: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen1084" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1085" type="x-p"/> Took ten camels - It appears that Abraham had left the whole management of this business to the discretion of his servant, to take with him what retinue and what dowry he pleased; for it is added, All the goods of his master were in his hand; and in those times it was customary to give a dowry for a wife, and not to receive one with her.
entries.ac95a5e097d4e9b9412aa10cd449461773669d61: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen1085" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1086" type="x-p"/> He made his camels to kneel down - To rest themselves, or lie down, as the Septuagint has very properly expressed it, Και εκοιμισε τας καμηλους. <div eID="gen1086" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1087" type="x-p"/> The time that women go out to draw water - In Bengal it is the universal practice for the women to go to pools and rivers to fetch water. Companies of four, six, ten, or more, may be seen in every town daily going to fetch water, with the pitchers resting upon their sides; and, on their return from bathing, women frequently bring water home - Ward.
entries.5c105e530194f70156f4823992d3335ab1ea15e8: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen1087" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1088" type="x-p"/> And he said, O Lord God, etc. - "The conduct of this servant," says Dr. Dodd, "appears no less pious than rational. By supplicating for a sign, he acknowledges God to be the great superintendent and director of the universe, and of that event in particular; and at the same time, by asking a natural sign, such as betokened humanity, condescension, and other qualities which promised a discreet and virtuous wife, he puts his prayer upon such a discreet, rational footing, as to be a proper example for all to imitate who would not tempt the providence of God, by expecting extraordinary signs to be given them for the determination of cases which they are capable of deciding by a proper use of their rational faculties." This is all very good; but certainly the case referred to here is such a one as required especial direction from God; a case which no use of the rational faculties, without Divine influence, could be sufficient to determine. It is easy to run into extremes, and it is very natural so to do. In all things the assistance and blessing of God are necessary, even where human strength and wisdom have the fullest and freest sphere of action; but there are numberless cases, of infinite consequence to man, where his strength and prudence can be of little or no avail, and where the God of all grace must work all things according to the counsel of his own will. To expect the accomplishment of any good end, without a proper use of the means, is the most reprehensible enthusiasm; and to suppose that any good can be done or procured without the blessing and mercy of God, merely because proper means are used, is not less reprehensible. Plan, scheme, and labor like Eliezer, and then, by earnest faith and prayer, commit the whole to the direction and blessing of God.
entries.613f2e0d9bf175300242be21abaded08972371fa: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen1088" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1089" type="x-p"/> Behold, Rebekah came out - How admirably had the providence of God adapted every circumstance to the necessity of the case, and so as in the most punctual manner to answer the prayer which his servant had offered up!
entries.cc6a39f6af7c6119cf16222fad16516197cea32a: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen1089" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1090" type="x-p"/> I will draw water for thy camels also - Had Rebekah done no more than Eliezer had prayed for, we might have supposed that she acted not as a free agent, but was impelled to it by the absolutely controlling power of God; but as she exceeds all that was requested, we see that it sprang from her native benevolence, and sets her conduct in the most amiable point of view.
entries.2406d0d2b76aaff90612032f1f824ced9bb50627: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen1090" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1091" type="x-p"/> The man, wondering at her - And he was so lost in wonder and astonishment at her simplicity, innocence, and benevolence, that he permitted this delicate female to draw water for ten camels, without ever attempting to afford her any kind of assistance! I know not which to admire most, the benevolence and condescension of Rebekah, or the cold and apparently stupid indifference of the servant of Abraham. Surely they are both of an uncommon cast.
entries.32545b808b09eebd7ac4aa1d25681e1819d35231: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen1091" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1092" type="x-p"/> The man took a golden ear-ring - נזם זהב nezem zahab. That this could not be an ear-ring is very probable from its being in the singular number. The margin calls it a jewel for the forehead; but it most likely means a jewel for the nose, or nose-ring, which is in universal use through all parts of Arabia and Persia, particularly among young women. They are generally worn in the left nostril. The word is very properly translated επιρῥινιον, an ornament for the nose, by Symmachus. <div eID="gen1092" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1093" type="x-p"/> Half a shekel - For the weight of a shekel, See note <reference osisRef="Gen.20.16">Gen 20:16</reference>. <div eID="gen1093" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1094" type="x-p"/> And two bracelets - ושני צמידים usheney tsemidim.
