Thus, although he conducted himself as became an honest and prudent servant, it is still not to be doubted that the Lord impelled him, for Isaac’s sake, to act as he did. So the Lord watches over his own people while they sleep, expedites and accomplishes their affairs in their absence, and influences the dispositions of all, so far as is expedient, to render them assistance. It is by a forced interpretation, that some would explain the ten days, during which Laban and his mother desire the departure of Rebekah to be deferred, as meaning years or months. For it was merely the tender wish of the mother, who could ill bear that her daughter should thus suddenly be torn away from her bosom.<div eID="gen3184" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Gen.24.54" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen3183" osisID="Gen.24.54" type="section"/>
entries.0fed895c416786468262946119acd0aab27fac1a: <div annotateRef="Bible:Gen.24.57" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Gen.24.57" sID="gen3185" type="section"/> <div sID="gen3186" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">57. </hi><hi type="italic">We will call the damsel</hi>. Bethuel, who had before unreservedly given his daughter in marriage, now seems to adhere, with but little constancy, to his purpose. When, however, he had previously offered his daughter, without making any exception, he is to be understood as having done it, only so far as he was able. But now, Moses declares that he did not exercise tyranny over his daughter, so as to thrust her out reluctantly, or to compel her to marry against her will, but left her to her own free choice. Truly, in this matter, the authority of parents ought to be sacred: but a middle course is to be pursued, so that the parties concerned may make their contract spontaneously, and with mutual consent. It is not right to understand that Rebekah in answering so explicitly, showed contempt for the paternal roof, or too anxiously desired a husband; <note n="11"> <div sID="gen3187" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="la">Vel procax juvencula maritum nimis cupide appeteret</foreign>.”<div eID="gen3187" type="x-p"/> </note> but since she saw that the affair was transacted by the authority of her father, and with the consent of her mother, she also herself acquiesced in it.<div eID="gen3186" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Gen.24.57" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen3185" osisID="Gen.24.57" type="section"/>
entries.e59ee74a6052ed82692274ca6a311571350f0093: <div annotateRef="Bible:Gen.24.59" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Gen.24.59" sID="gen3188" type="section"/> <div sID="gen3189" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">59. </hi><hi type="italic">And they sent away Rebekah</hi>. Moses first relates, that Rebekah was honorably dismissed; because her nurse was given unto her. Moreover, I doubt not that they had domestic nurses, who were their handmaidens; not that mothers entirely neglected that duty, but that they committed the care of education to one particular maid. They therefore who assisted mothers with subsidiary service were called nurses. Moses afterwards adds, that Rebekah’s relatives “blessed her,” (<reference osisRef="Bible:Gen.24.60">Genesis 24:60</reference>,) by which expression he means, that they prayed that her condition might be a happy one. We know that it was a solemn custom, in all ages, and among all people, to accompany marriages with all good wishes. And although posterity has greatly degenerated from the pure and genuine method of celebrating marriages used by the fathers; yet it is God’s will that some public testimony should stand forth, by which men may be admonished, that no nuptials are lawful, except those which are rightly consecrated. Now, the particular form of benediction which is here related, was probably in common use, because nature dictates that the propagation of offspring is the special end of marriage. Under the notion of victory (<reference osisRef="Bible:Gen.24.60">Genesis 24:60</reference>) is comprehended a prosperous state of life. The Lord, however, directed their tongues to utter a prophecy of which they themselves were ignorant. To possess the gates of enemies, means to obtain dominion over them; because judgment was administered in the gates, and the bulwarks of the city were placed there.<div eID="gen3189" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Gen.24.59" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen3188" osisID="Gen.24.59" type="section"/>
entries.11212b182ddba6dffba276dfd6bdd1a49c651d74: <div annotateRef="Bible:Gen.24.63" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Gen.24.63" sID="gen3190" type="section"/> <div sID="gen3191" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">63. </hi><hi type="italic">And Isaac went out</hi>. It appears that Isaac dwelt apart from his father; either because the family was too large, or because such was the custom. And perhaps Abraham had already married another wife; so that, for the sake of avoiding contentions, it would seem more convenient for him to have a house of his own. Thus great wealth has its attendant troubles. Doubtless, of all earthly blessings granted by God, none would have been sweeter to Abraham than that of living with his son. However, I by no means think that he was deprived of his society and assistance. For such was the piety of Isaac, that he undoubtedly studied to discharge every duty towards his father: this alone was wanting, that they did not live in the same house. Moses also relates how it happened that Isaac met with his wife before she reached his home. For he says, that Isaac went out in the evening to <hi type="italic">meditate</hi> or to <hi type="italic">pray</hi>. For the Hebrew word <foreign xml:lang="he">שוח</foreign> (<hi type="italic">soach</hi>) may mean either. It is probable that he did this according to his custom, and that he sought a place of retirement for prayer, in order that his mind, being released from all avocations, might be the more at liberty to serve God. Whether, however, he was giving his mind to meditation or to prayer, the Lord granted him a token of his own presence in that joyful meeting.<div eID="gen3191" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Gen.24.63" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen3190" osisID="Gen.24.63" type="section"/>
entries.b8689d22017fa904f2a29154cb9d31203546bd27: <div annotateRef="Bible:Gen.24.64" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Gen.24.64" sID="gen3192" type="section"/> <div sID="gen3193" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">64. </hi><hi type="italic">And Rebekah lifted up her eyes</hi>. We may easily conjecture that Isaac, when he saw the camels, turned his steps towards them, from the desire of seeing his bride; this gave occasion to the inquiry of Rebekah. Having received the answer, she immediately, for the sake of doing honor to her husband, dismounted her camel to salute him. For that she fell, struck with fear, as some suppose, in no way agrees with the narrative. She had performed too long a journey, under the protection of many attendants, to be so greatly afraid at the sight of one man. But these interpreters are deceived, because they do not perceive, that in the words of Moses, the reason is afterwards given to this effect, that when Rebekah saw Isaac, she alighted from her camel; because she had inquired of the servant who he was, and had been told that he was the son of his master Abraham. It would not have entered into her mind to make such inquiry respecting any person whom she might accidentally meet: but seeing she had been informed that Abraham’s house was not far distant, she supposes him at least to be one of the domestics. Moses also says that she took a veil: which was a token of shame and modesty. For hence also, the Latin word which signifies “to marry,” <note n="12"> <div sID="gen3194" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="la">Verbum nubendi</foreign>.” The original meaning of the word <foreign xml:lang="la">nubere</foreign> is <hi type="italic">to veil</hi>, or <hi type="italic">cover</hi>.<div eID="gen3194" type="x-p"/> </note> is derived, because it was the custom to give brides veiled to their husbands. That the same rite was also observed by the fathers, I have no doubt. <note n="13"> <div sID="gen3195" type="x-p"/> “Isaac was walking, and it would therefore have been the highest breach of Oriental good manners, to have remained on the camel when presented to him. No doubt they all alighted and walked to meet him, conducting Rebekah as a bride to meet the bridegroom.” — <hi type="italic">Bush</hi>. — <hi type="italic">Ed</hi>.<div eID="gen3195" type="x-p"/> </note> So much the more shameful, and the less capable of excuse, is the licentiousness of our own age; in which the apparel of brides seems to be purposely contrived for the subversion of all modesty.<div eID="gen3193" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Gen.24.64" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen3192" osisID="Gen.24.64" type="section"/>

67. And Isaac brought her into his mother Sarah’s tent. He first brought her into the tent, then took her as his wife. By the very arrangement of his words, Moses distinguishes between the legitimate mode of marriage and barbarism. And certainly the sanctity of marriage demands that man and woman should not live together like cattle; but that, having pledged their mutual faith, and invoked the name of God, they might dwell with each other. Besides, it is to be observed, that Isaac was not compelled, by the tyrannical command of his father, to marry; but after he had given his mind to her he took her freely, and cordially gave her the assurance of conjugal fidelity.
And Isaac was comforted after his mother’s death. Since his grief for the death of his mother was now first assuaged, we infer how great had been its vehemence; for a period sufficiently long had already elapsed.
The time from the death of Sarah to Isaac’s marriage was three years. — Ed.
We may also hence infer, that the affection of Isaac was tender and gentle: and that his love to his mother was of no common kind, seeing he had so long lamented her death. And the knowledge of this fact is useful to prevent us from imagining that the holy patriarchs were men of savage manners and of iron hardness of heart, and from becoming like those who conceive fortitude to consist in brutality. Only care must be taken that grief should be duly mitigated; lest it burst forth in impious murmurings, or subvert the hope of a future resurrection. I do not however entirely excuse the sorrow of Isaac; I only advise, that what belongs to humanity, ought not to be altogether condemned. And although it was culpable not to be able to efface grief from the mind, until the opposite joy of marriage prevailed over it; Moses still reckons it among the benefits conferred by God, that he applies a remedy of any kind to his servant.

                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> good of countenance.</ns0:note> very fair to look upon, a virgin, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Numb. 31. 17.</ns0:note> neither had any man known her <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">(<ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi>) She was a Virgin not onely in Title and shew, but in Truth, for no man had known her, <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> corrupted her.</ns0:note>: and she went down to the well, and filled her pit<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cher, and came up.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="17">17 And the servant ran to meet her, and said, Let me (I pray thee) drink a little water of thy pitcher.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="18">18 And she said, drink my Lord <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">For his retinue shewed him to be a person of more than ordinary quality.</ns0:note>; and she hasted, and let down her pitcher upon her hand, and gave him drink.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="19">19 And when she had done giving him drink, she said, I will draw <ns0:hi>water</ns0:hi> for thy camels also, until they have done drinking.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="20">20 And she hasted, and emptied her pitcher in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />to the trough, and ran again unto the well to draw <ns0:hi>water,</ns0:hi> and drew for all his camels.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="21">21 And the man wondring at her <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">(<ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi>) At the wonderful providence of God and the emi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nent answer of his prayer.</ns0:note>, held his peace, to wit, that he might know whether the LORD had made his journey prosperous, or not.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="22">22 And it came to pass, as the camels had done drinking; that the man took <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">(<ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi>) Gave to her, as that word of <ns0:hi>taking,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>receiving</ns0:hi> is oft used, as <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 12. 19. <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 18. 12. and 29. 25. <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 68. 18. compared with <ns0:hi>Eph.</ns0:hi> 4. 8.</ns0:note> a golden <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Or,</ns0:hi> jewel for the forehead.</ns0:note> ear<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ring <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">So the word signifies, <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 35. 4. <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 32. 2, 3. Or <ns0:hi>jewels for the forehead,</ns0:hi> which hung down from the forehead to the nose, or between the eyes. So the word is used, <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 47. <ns0:hi>Ezek.</ns0:hi> 16. 12.</ns0:note> of half a shekel weight, and two brace<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lets for her hands, of ten <ns0:hi>shekels</ns0:hi> weight of gold.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="23">23 And said <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>For he had said:</ns0:hi> For it is probable he enquired who she was before he gave her those presents.</ns0:note>, whose daughter <ns0:hi>art</ns0:hi> thou? tell me, I pray thee: is there room in thy fathers house for us to lodge in?</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="24">24 And she said unto him, I <ns0:hi>am</ns0:hi> the daughter of Bethuel, the son of Milcah <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">So she signifies that she was Nahors Daughter not by his Concubine, but by his lawful and principal Wife.</ns0:note>, which she bare un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />to Nahor:</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="25">25 She said moreover unto him, we have both straw and provender enough, and room to lodge in.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="26">26 And the man bowed down his head, and worshipped the LORD <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Giving thanks to God for his marvellous assistance hither<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />to, and begging the continuance of his presence and blessing.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="27">27 And he said, blessed be the LORD God of my Master Abraham; who hath not left destitute my master of his mercy, and his truth <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">(<ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi>) Who hath shewed his <ns0:hi>mercy</ns0:hi> in promising all man<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ner of blessings, and his <ns0:hi>truth</ns0:hi> in performing his promises at this day. Or it is a figure called <ns0:hi>Hendyadis,</ns0:hi> for <ns0:hi>true mercy, q. d.</ns0:hi> he hath not onely been kind to him in shew and in words but in real and considerable effects.</ns0:note>: I <ns0:hi>being</ns0:hi> in the way, the LORD led me to the house of my masters brethren <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">(<ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi>) Near Kinsmen, as that word is commonly used, as <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 48. and <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 13. 8. <ns0:hi>Mark</ns0:hi> 3. 31, 32.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="28">28 And the damsel ran, and told <ns0:hi>them</ns0:hi> of her mothers house <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">Not, <ns0:hi>of her Fathers house;</ns0:hi> either because her Father was now dead, and <ns0:hi>Bethuel,</ns0:hi> who is hereafter mentioned, was not <ns0:hi>L<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                              <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                           </ns0:gap>bans</ns0:hi> Father, but his Brother so called: Or because the Wo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />men had distinct appartiments in the houses, and she went first thither according to her custom.</ns0:note> these things.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="29">29 And Rebekah had a brother, and his name <ns0:hi>was</ns0:hi> Laban, and Laban ran out unto the man unto the well.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="30">30 And it came to pass, when he saw the ear<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ring, and bracelets upon his sisters hands, and when he heard the words of Rebekah his sister, saying, Thus spake the man unto me; that he came unto the man, and behold he stood by the camels at the well.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="31">31 And he said, Come in thou blessed of the LORD <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">(<ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi>) Whom God hath so eminently favoured and blessed.</ns0:note>, wherefore standest thou without? for I have prepared the house, and room for the ca<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mels.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="32">
                     <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:25" />32 And the man came into the house, and he ungirded his camels, and gave straw and provender for the camels, and water to wash his feet, and the <ns0:hi>mens</ns0:hi> feet that <ns0:hi>were</ns0:hi> with him <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">Of which custom, see <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 18. 4.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="33">33 And there was set <ns0:hi>meat</ns0:hi> before him, to eat: but he said, I will not eat untill I have told mine errand. And he said, speak on.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="34">34 And he said, I <ns0:hi>am</ns0:hi> Abrahams servant.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="35">35 And the LORD hath blessed my master great<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ly, and he is become great; and he hath given him flocks, and herds, and silver, and gold, and men-servants, and maid-servants, and camels, and asses.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="36">36 And Sarah my masters wife bare a son to my master when she was old, and <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 25. 5.</ns0:note> unto him hath he given all that he hath <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">(<ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi>) Hath purposed and promised, and doth by me en<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gage that he will give. Things are oft said to be done, in Scrip<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ture language, when they will certainly and shortly be done.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="37">37 And my master made me swear, saying, thou shalt not take a wife to my son of the daughters of the Canaanites, in whole land I dwell.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="38">38 But thou shalt go unto my Fathers house, and to my kindred, and take a wife unto my son.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="39">39 And I said unto my master, Peradventure the woman will not follow me.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="40">40 And he said unto me, The LORD, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 17. 1.</ns0:note> before whom I walk <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">In Obedience to all his commands, and in hearty trust in his promises and gracious providence towards me and mine.</ns0:note>, will send his angel with thee, and prosper thy way: and thou shalt take a wife for my son of my kindred, and of my fathers house.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="41">41 Then shalt thou be clear from <ns0:hi>this</ns0:hi> my oath <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">Heb. <ns0:hi>from my curse,</ns0:hi> denounced against thee if thou shouldst violate thine oath. The words <ns0:hi>oath</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>curse</ns0:hi> are oft-times in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />differently used because they commonly go together, and some<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />times they are both expressed, as <ns0:hi>Numb.</ns0:hi> 5. 21.</ns0:note>, when thou comest to my kindred, and if they give not thee <ns0:hi>one,</ns0:hi> thou shalt be clear from my oath.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="42">42 And I came this day unto the well, and said, O LORD God of my master Abraham, if now thou do prosper my way which I go <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">(<ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi>) The design or course in which I am ingaged: as the word <ns0:hi>way</ns0:hi> is frequently used.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="43">43 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Vers. 13.</ns0:note> Behold, I stand by the well of water, and it shall come to pass, that when the Virgin cometh forth to draw <ns0:hi>water,</ns0:hi> and I say to her, Give me, I pray thee, a little water of thy pitcher to drink.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="44">44 And she say to me, Both drink thou, and I will also draw for thy camels: <ns0:hi>let</ns0:hi> the same <ns0:hi>be</ns0:hi> the woman, whom the LORD hath appointed out for my masters son.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="45">45 And before I had done speaking in my heart, behold, Rebekah came forth with her pit<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cher on her shoulder, and she went down unto the well, and drew <ns0:hi>water:</ns0:hi> and I said unto her, Let me drink, I pray thee.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="46">46 And she made haste, and let down her pit<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cher from her <ns0:hi>shoulder,</ns0:hi> and said, drink, and I will give thy camels drink also: so I drank, and she made the camels drink also.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="47">47 And I asked her <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">First he asks who she was, then he gives the gifts to her: Which is the right order and is here observed in the repetition. which was inverted in the first relation, <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 22, 23.</ns0:note>, and said, whose daugh<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ter <ns0:hi>art</ns0:hi> thou? and she said, the daughter of Bethuel Nahors son, whom Milcah bare unto him: and I put the ear-ring upon her face, and the brace<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lets upon her hands.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="48">48 And I bowed down my head, and worship<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ped the LORD, and blessed the LORD God of my master Abraham, which had led me in <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> the way of <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>.</ns0:note> the right way, to take my masters brothers daughter unto his son.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="49">49 And now if ye will deal kindly and truly <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">If you will shew true kindness and real friendship to him in giving your daughter to his son.</ns0:note> with my master, tell me: and if not, tell me, that I may turn to the right hand, or to the left <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">(<ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi>) That I may look out a wife for him elsewhere. It is a proverbial expression, <ns0:hi>Numb.</ns0:hi> 20. 17. and 22. 26. <ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 2. 27.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="50">50 Then Laban and Bethuel <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>Laban</ns0:hi> is put first, either because this <ns0:hi>Bethuel</ns0:hi> was not his Fa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther but his younger Brother, as <ns0:hi>Iosephus</ns0:hi> thinks; or because <ns0:hi>Laban</ns0:hi> was the chief manager of this business, to whom his Fa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther seems to have committed the care of his Family being him<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />self unfit for it through age or infirmity.</ns0:note> answered and said, The thing proceedeth from the LORD <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">From Gods coun<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sel and special providence. Hereby it appears they had the Knowledge and Worship of the true God among them, though they added Idols to him.</ns0:note>: we cannot speak unto thee bad or good <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">We cannot without opposing God speak or act any thing which may hinder thy design or thwart thy desires. Compare <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 31. 24, 29. 2 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 13. 22.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="51">51 Behold, Rebekah <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> before thee <ns0:note n="‖" place="bottom">(<ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi>) In thy power and disposal; as this phrase is ta<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ken <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 20. 15. and elsewhere.</ns0:note>, take <ns0:hi>her,</ns0:hi> and go, and let her be thy masters sons wife, as the LORD hath spoken.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="52">52 And it came to pass, that when Abrahams servant heard their words, he worshipped the LORD, <ns0:hi>bowing himself</ns0:hi> to the Earth.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="53">53 And the servant brought forth <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> vessels.</ns0:note> jewels of silver, and jewels of gold, and raiment, and gave <ns0:hi>them</ns0:hi> to Rebekah: he gave also to her brother, and to her mother precious things <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">The precious fruits of the Land from which he came. See <ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 33. 13, &c. or in general, other rare and excellent things. In those dayes men gave portions for their wives, as now they have portions with them.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="54">54 And they did eat and drink, he, and the men that <ns0:hi>were</ns0:hi> with him, and tarried all night: and they rose up in the morning, and he said, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Vers. 56. and 59.</ns0:note> send me away unto my master.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="55">55 And her brother and her mother said, let the damsel abide with us <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>a full year,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>ten</ns0:hi> months.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:hi>a few</ns0:hi> days, at the least ten <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">Others thus, <ns0:hi>a year, or</ns0:hi> at the least <ns0:hi>ten</ns0:hi> months, the word <ns0:hi>days</ns0:hi> being put for a year, as elsewhere. But it is very im<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />probable that they would demand or expect such a thing from this man whom they saw bent so much upon expedition.</ns0:note>, after that she shall go.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="56">56 And he said unto them, hinder me not, see<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing the LORD hath prospered my way: send me away, that I may go to my master.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="57">57 And they said, we will call the damsel, and inquire at her mouth <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">(<ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi>) Understand her mind by her words, not so much concerning the marriage it self, in which she resigned up her self to the disposal of her Parents and Friends, and to which she had given an implicit consent by her acceptance of those presents which were made to her for that end; as concern<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing the hastiness of her departure.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="58">58 And they called Rebekah, and said unto her, wilt thou go with this man? And she said, I will go.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="59">59 And they sent away Rebekah their sister, and her nurse <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>Deborah,</ns0:hi> by comparing <ns0:hi>chap.</ns0:hi> 35. 8. In this corrupt Fa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mily the Mother and the Nurse are two distinct persons, but in <ns0:hi>Abrahams</ns0:hi> pious Family there was no such principle or pra<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ctise. See <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 21. 7.</ns0:note>, and Abrahams servant; and his men.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="60">60 And they blessed Rebekah, and said unto her, Thou <ns0:hi>art</ns0:hi> our sister <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">(<ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi>) Our near Kinswoman, distance of place shall not alienate our affections from thee, but we shall still own thee as our sister, and, as far as we can, be ready to perform all the du<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ties of brethren to thee.</ns0:note>, be thou <ns0:hi>the mother</ns0:hi> of thousands of millions, and <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 22. 17.</ns0:note> let thy seed possesse the gate of those which hate them.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="61">
                     <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:26" />61 And Rebekah arose, and her damsels, and they rode upon the camels, and followed the man: and the servant took Rebekah, and went his way.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="62">62 And Isaac came from the way of the<ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 16. 14. and 25. 11.</ns0:note> well Lahai-roi, for he dwelt in the south-country<ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">In the Southern part of <ns0:hi>Canaan,</ns0:hi> as <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 12. 9. at <ns0:hi>Beer<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sheba</ns0:hi> whither, it seems, <ns0:hi>Abraham</ns0:hi> returned after <ns0:hi>Sarahs</ns0:hi> death.</ns0:note>
                  </ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="63">63 And Isaac went out to<ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Or,</ns0:hi> to pray.</ns0:note> meditate<ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">To converse with God and with himself by pious and profita<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ble thoughts and ejaculations, and fervent prayers, as for other things, so particularly for Gods blessing upon this great affair, and so his prayers are eminently answered.</ns0:note> in the field<ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">He chuseth a solitary place, wherein he might more freely attend upon God without any interruption or distraction.</ns0:note> at the even-tide<ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">That as he had begun the day with God, so he might close it with him, and commit himself to his protection. Compare <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 55. 17.</ns0:note>: and he lift up his eyes, and saw, and behold, the camels <ns0:hi>were</ns0:hi> coming.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="64">64 And Rebekah lift up her eyes, and when she saw Isaac, she lighted off the camel<ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">As a testimony of her respect to him whom by the servant she understood to be her Lord and Husband. Compare <ns0:hi>Ios.</ns0:hi> 15. 18. 1 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 25. 23.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="65">65 For she had said unto the servant, what man <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> this that walketh in the field to meet us? And the servant had said, It <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> my master: there<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fore she took a vail, and covered her self<ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">In token of modesty, reverence, and subjection. See <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 20. 16. 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 11. 10.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="66">66 And the servant told Isaac all things that he had done.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="67">67 And Isaac brought her into his mother Sa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rahs tent<ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">Partly to give her possession of it, and partly to consum<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mate the Marriage. Women then had their tents apart from Men. See <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 18. 10. and 24. 67. and 31. 33.</ns0:note>, and took Rebekah, and she became his wife, and he loved her, and Isaac was com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />forted after his mothers <ns0:hi>death</ns0:hi>
                     <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">A sor<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rowful sense whereof he yet had retained though she died three years before this time.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               </ns0:div>
